specPoints.text: understand, in terms of bond enthalpy, the trend in reactivity of chloro-, bromo- and iodoalkanes

primer.text: Polarity promises fluorine, bond strength delivers iodine. This note weighs the two factors behind halogenoalkane reactivity, shows why the strongest polar bond is the hardest to break, and lands the ladder where substitution rates actually fall: iodide first, fluoride barely at all.

lessons.title: Polarity and the reactivity puzzle
lessons.opening: Electronegativity says fluoroalkanes should react fastest - the C-F bond is the most polar, so carbon looks most attackable. Reality inverts the prediction, and the deciding factor is bond strength, which wins over polarity every time.
keyPoints: The C-X bond is polar: carbon carries d+ and halogen d-, from the electronegativity difference.
Electronegativity falls down the group, so bond polarity also falls.
Polarity alone would suggest fluoroalkanes react quickest.
Bond strength is the greater factor and reverses the prediction.

low.restatement: The polarity ladder runs F strongest to I weakest, but the bond-enthalpy ladder runs the other way and carries more weight - so iodoalkanes, not fluoroalkanes, react fastest.
low.analogy: Two scoreboards disagree: polarity cheers fluorine, bond strength cheers iodine - and bond strength holds the tiebreaker.
low.examPointer: Name BOTH factors when explaining the reactivity trend, and state explicitly that bond enthalpy dominates polarity.

medium.restatement: The d+ carbon invites nucleophiles in every halogenoalkane; what differs is how easily the C-X bond can be broken once the nucleophile arrives. Weaker bonds (C-I) yield faster than strong ones (C-F).
medium.analogy: Every door looks open from outside (polarity), but the hinges differ (bond strength): the rustiest hinges swing first.
medium.examPointer: Answer 'why does the prediction fail?' with the bond-enthalpy override, not with a denial of polarity.

check.stem: Which factor would, on its own, suggest fluoroalkanes react fastest?

options.text: Bond polarity, since C-F is the most polarised bond
options.explanation: Strongest electronegativity difference means the most d+ carbon.

options.text: Bond enthalpy, since C-F is the strongest bond
options.explanation: That factor argues fluoroalkanes are slowest.

options.text: Molar mass, since fluorine is lightest
options.explanation: Mass is not the deciding factor here.

options.text: Atomic radius, since fluorine is smallest
options.explanation: Radius feeds polarity, but the stated factor is the polarity consequence.

check.stem: Why does the polarity prediction fail?

options.text: Bond strength is the greater factor: strong C-F resists breaking despite its polarity
options.explanation: The rate is set by how easily the bond breaks, not how polar it is.
It is the most electronegative element.
They are the most polar of the series.
Nucleophiles seek polar bonds' d+ carbons.

check.stem: The carbon in every C-X bond carries

options.explanation: Electronegativity difference pulls electrons toward the halogen.
That is the halogen's side.
Covalent bonds share, polarising only partially.
Polarity gives partial charges by definition.

check.stem: As electronegativity decreases down Group 7, the polarity of the C-X bond

options.text: Also decreases, from C-F to C-I
options.explanation: Smaller electronegativity difference means weaker polarisation.
Length does not increase polarity here.
The difference in electronegativity changes steadily.
It remains a contributing factor, just not the dominant one.

check.stem: Which order does bond strength give for halogenoalkane reactivity?

options.explanation: Bond enthalpy, falling from C-F to C-I, sets the order.
That is the polarity-only prediction, which fails.
Commonness is not a reactivity factor.
The bond strengths differ greatly.

check.stem: State the two factors affecting halogenoalkane reactivity.
check.modelAnswer: Bond polarity (suggesting fluorine fastest) and bond strength (the greater factor, making iodine fastest).

check.stem: State the direction of the polarity trend down the halogen series.
check.modelAnswer: Bond polarity decreases from C-F to C-I as electronegativity falls.

check.stem: Explain why the C-F bond's polarity does not make fluoroalkanes reactive.
check.modelAnswer: Although the bond is strongly polarised, its very high bond enthalpy means nucleophiles cannot break it, so strength overrides polarity in setting the rate.

check.stem: A student predicts fluoroalkanes react fastest 'because carbon is most positive there'. Write the correction.
check.modelAnswer: The d+ carbon does attract nucleophiles, but the rate depends on breaking the C-X bond; C-F is the strongest carbon-halogen bond, so fluoroalkanes are actually the least reactive.

lessons.title: Bond enthalpy decides the race
lessons.opening: Substitution means breaking the carbon-halogen bond, so the bond energies write the reactivity ladder: C-I needs least energy and breaks first, C-F needs most and resists. Iodoethane with hydroxide shows the weakest bond falling fastest.
keyPoints: Every substitution must break the carbon-halogen bond, so bond energies explain the different reactivities.
The C-I bond demands the least break energy of the series, making it the weakest carbon-halogen bond.
The C-F bond requires the most energy and is the strongest carbon-halogen bond.
Iodoalkanes break heterolytically fastest: CH3CH2I + OH- -> CH3CH2OH + I-.

low.restatement: Rank the bonds by breakability - C-I easiest, then C-Br, C-Cl, C-F hardest - and the hydrolysis speed ladder follows exactly; the leaving halide departs with the bond's electron pair.
low.analogy: Four padlocks cut with increasing difficulty: iodine's is tin snips, fluorine's needs bolt cutters - the snips win every race.
low.examPointer: Tie the trend to the heterolytic departure: the pair goes with the halogen, and weaker bonds surrender their pair sooner.

medium.restatement: Bond enthalpy is the energy toll for the rate-determining break; down the group the bond lengthens and weakens, so iodoalkanes clear the toll first. The fluoroalkane's toll is so high it barely reacts at all.
medium.analogy: Toll booths on the substitution road: iodine charges pennies, fluorine charges a fortune - traffic flows accordingly.
medium.examPointer: Quote the iodoethane equation with OH- as the canonical fastest case.

check.stem: Which carbon-halogen bond is the weakest?

options.text: C-I, requiring the least energy to break
options.explanation: Iodine's large, long bond surrenders its pair most easily.
C-F is the strongest, not the weakest.
Chloride middles the ladder.
The bond enthalpies differ substantially.

check.stem: During substitution, the carbon-halogen bond breaks

options.text: Heterolytically, both electrons leaving with the halide
options.explanation: The pair departs with the electronegative halogen as X-.

options.text: Homolytically, one electron to each atom
options.explanation: No radicals form in this substitution.
The pair must go somewhere - it leaves with X.

options.text: Only in the presence of a catalyst
options.explanation: No catalyst is involved.

options.text: The C-F bond is the strongest carbon-halogen bond
options.explanation: High bond enthalpy blocks the rate-determining break.
Repulsion is not the mechanism; energy cost is.
Solubility is not the stated cause.
C-F bonds are common and stable.

check.stem: In CH3CH2I + OH- -> CH3CH2OH + I-, the hydroxide

options.text: Replaces the iodine on carbon, taking the alcohol's oxygen position
options.explanation: The substitution installs OH where I departed.
No oxidation change occurs; it is substitution.
Iodoethane has no double bond.

options.text: Acts as a base removing hydrogen iodide
options.explanation: That describes elimination, not this substitution.

check.stem: Why does bond strength set the pace of substitution?

options.text: The rate-determining step requires breaking the C-X bond, so its energy sets the pace
options.explanation: Polarity attracts the nucleophile, but breakability times the reaction.

options.text: Polarity does not exist in these bonds
options.explanation: It does; it is simply outweighed.

options.text: Bond enthalpy is easier to measure
options.explanation: Measurement convenience is not the mechanistic reason.
The physics of the rate-determining break decides.

check.stem: State the bond-enthalpy order for the carbon-halogen series.
check.modelAnswer: C-F strongest, then C-Cl, C-Br, with C-I the weakest.

check.stem: Write the substitution equation for iodoethane with hydroxide.
check.modelAnswer: CH3CH2I + OH- -> CH3CH2OH + I-, the fastest hydrolysis of the series.

check.stem: Explain why iodoalkanes react fastest with nucleophiles.
check.modelAnswer: The C-I bond has the lowest bond enthalpy, so the rate-determining break happens soonest, liberating iodide and completing substitution fastest.

check.stem: Predict which halogenoalkane hydrolyses fastest among C2H5Cl, C2H5Br and C2H5I, and justify without naming bond enthalpies.
check.modelAnswer: C2H5I: iodine is the largest halogen, its bond to carbon is longest and easiest to break, so the iodoalkane surrenders its halide first.

glossary.definition: The unequal sharing of electrons in the C-X bond giving carbon d+ and halogen d-.
The energy required to break a bond; the decisive factor in halogenoalkane reactivity.
Bond breaking in which the electron pair departs with the halogen as X-.
